newsitem.title: UK: UK seeks new powers to stop illegal beef exports.
newsitem.headline: UK seeks new powers to stop illegal beef exports.

text.p: The government said on Tuesday that it would use extra powers to curb illegal exports of British beef in defiance of the worldwide ban imposed by the European Union.
The move followed allegations by the European Commission that attempts had been made to export 1,650 tonnes of beef to Bosnia, Poland, Equatorial Guinea, Egypt and Russia.

Agriculture Minister Jack Cunningham said he would introduce legislation into parliament to "clarify and strengthen the powers available to UK officials where illegal exports are suspected," and to improve checks carried out at ports.
Cunningham on Monday announced the closure of two meat plants in Britain on suspicion they were involved in breaking the worldwide ban on exports.
He said on Tuesday that his officials were cooperating with the EU regarding the allegations of illegal exports, and criminal proceedings would be taken if necessary.

"In light of recent events, I have undertaken a thorough review of the measures currently in place to implement the ban on the export of UK beef," Cunningham said in a written answer to a parliamentary question.

Earlier in Moscow, British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said a Belgian company was apparently responsible for the smuggling, but he fully accepted that the beef should not have left Britain in the first place.

Blaming the previous Conservative government for its reaction to mad cow disease, he said: "We are not satisfied that, in this case, as in so many other cases of the Conservatives' response to the beef crisis, that their measures were adequate."
Cunningham said the extra steps he was now taking were essential to get the EU export ban lifted.
"The UK is under an obligation to implement and enforce the export ban firmly and effectively for as long as it is in place," he said.
"Only in this way will we regain the trust of our European partners, which is an essential pre-requisite to an early lifting of the export ban."

The worldwide ban was imposed in March 1996 because of evidence that mad cow disease may be transmitted to humans through infected beef. Britain has instituted a widespread cull to remove BSE from the food chain.
